narrative:
The model determined that you have a 77% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the law school decided to reject your application.

Three factors drove this outcome most strongly. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the single biggest reason the model leaned toward failure. Placing in the bottom decile, far below the average of roughly sixth place among accepted students, signaled that your academic performance had not reached the level typically needed to pass the bar. Your LSAT score of 24 was the second most important factor; it sits well below the 37-point average of students who were admitted, pushing the prediction further toward failure. Finally, your first-year class ranking in the lowest decile, compared with an average around sixth place among accepted applicants, added additional weight in the same direction.

None of these features pulled the prediction toward success; all three worked together to increase the estimated risk of failing the bar. Your low family income, undergraduate GPA of 2.9, and other details played smaller roles.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Many students strengthen their profile this way and are admitted in a later cycle. Consider targeted bar-prep resources early so that when you do enroll, you are better prepared to pass on the first try.
